name: LevelUp
oneLiner: A clip-on bubble level for barbells, built for lifters who don't know they lift unevenly.

context.role: Grocery-bag research (interviews, competitor chart); the magnetic-level sketch; the business model canvas

blocks.title: My grocery bags lost to a barbell
blocks.text:
DSGN 308 makes you find your own problem. Our seven-person team pooled a 55-response survey, AEIOU sessions and our own complaints into 122 opportunities, kept the 44 a product could fix, and chased three: a messy machine shop, slipping grocery-bag straps, and the gym.

I was on groceries. I interviewed shoppers and built our chart of eight existing fixes. The verdict was polite: slipping straps ranked sixth of seven grocery gripes, and none of our ten interviewees brought them up. The gym pair had timed machine queues (4.5 minutes on average) and picked crooked bars instead, by half a point. Final matrix: gym 82.5, shop 70.5, groceries 63.

blocks.title: Common, unnoticed, and no cheap solo fix
blocks.text:
Two teammates spent an hour at SPAC, the campus gym: 30 minutes of AEIOU observation, then five interviews. Barbells were the busiest equipment, spotters were rare, and in 20 minutes three people lifted a visibly uneven bar. Most interviewees didn't see it as their problem, including one we had just watched do it.

A Northwestern lift coach said mild upper-body imbalance is usually fine, but in extreme cases a raised shoulder can lead to impingement, rotator-cuff trouble and, at worst, a torn labrum. The fixes on offer ran from a $274.99 barbell with a built-in level to a $3,999 smart gym, or another person watching you.

media.caption: Our benchmark of seven existing fixes, +1/0/−1 on cost, access, effectiveness, convenience and safety. Most cost money or need another person; dumbbells only help up to a point.

blocks.title: Everyone sees it — in someone else
blocks.text: “I don't personally have problems with it because I have good body control. I notice it in other people though.” — a gym-goer at SPAC, whom we had just watched bench unevenly

blocks.title: Every need got a number, eventually
blocks.text:
Our first spec sheet asked for “fits in pocket” and “universally understandable”; by the final report every need had a number. The final prototype, tested with three lifters at SPAC on June 10:

! Need | Spec | LevelUp
Visible | Testers rate how well they saw it: ≥ 4/5 | 4.35/5
Intuitive | On the bar without instructions in < 5 s | 2.5 s average
Unobstructive | Never touches the lifter | Hit 1 of 3 chests: miss
Portable | Fits an average gym bag | 2.76 × 1.34 × 1.21 in
Adaptable | 2+ exercises | 4 (we simulated them): bench, spotted squat, row, curl
Adaptable | Fits 28.5 mm bars ± 3 mm | 28.5 mm only: miss
Cost-effective | Unit cost < $10 | $1.30 or $3.90 (our figures differ): pass
Balance-effective | ≥ 90% of reps level | 100% (60% with the vial hidden)
Intentional | Each rep slows by > 1 s | 0.98 s: a miss the report rounded up

blocks.title: The obvious idea showed up six times
blocks.text:
We brainwrote alone first, ten ideas each, so no single voice set the direction: 70 ideas, then three sketches apiece, 21 in all. Lasers, accelerometers, phone apps and wearables all appeared, but six of our seven lists had a bubble level on them.

Mine had three, plus three ideas for marking where your hands go. I sketched a level vial capped with magnets, to stick straight onto a steel bar; magnets turned up on two other lists too, and the sketch made our final deck. We took three directions into mockups: a plain level, a phone running a level app, and a bearing that slides when the bar tips.

media.caption: My sketch for the May 11 concept round: a level vial capped with magnets.
A teammate's sketch: the phone as the level, clipped to the bar.
A teammate's sketch: bearing cuffs that slide into your hand when the bar tips.

blocks.title: Every audience crowned a different mockup
blocks.text:
We built cheap: cardboard, velcro, zip ties and a $5.99 five-pack of magnetic levels. The first two rounds (May 21–22) only tested how a level holds on. Magnets won; the shaft collars took too long, the velcro nearly hit a chin, and the magnetic tape we ordered wouldn't stick to the gym's bars.

Then we pitted three directions against each other. The lift coach preferred the bearing, our class the phone, gym-goers the plain level. We chose the level on our requirements: most intuitive, portable, cheapest and buildable in the time left. Its flaw came with it: a small bubble that rolls out of view as the bar turns.

media.caption: Round 1 (May 21), velcro on cardboard: easy on, but the straps nearly hit a tester's chin.
Round 2's 1-inch clip was the fastest on, but too big for the gym's bars, so it spun. The clip came back at the end.
The phone stand: the most responsive readout, until its magnets let go and the phone fell as a tester lowered the bar.
Bubble (left) against bearing (right): the bearing only started sliding after 0.7–2.7° of tilt, the bubble at once.
Lift-coach session: the bar met the coach's chest and the bubble split into several. Which one is level?
Final concept v1 (June 10): two levels on fabric, so one is always in view. The fabric let them twist out of line, and testers watched only one.

blocks.title: The losing mockup gave the winner its angle
blocks.text:
We rebuilt the level from scratch. LevelUp is a printed black PLA clip that snaps over the bar, with no straps or magnets, and a 1-inch vial press-fit on an arm standing just under an inch off the bar. That angle came from the phone stand we had dropped: testers kept tilting the phone forward to face them.

On June 10, three SPAC lifters clipped it on without instructions in 2.5 seconds on average. With the vial hidden, the bubble left the level zone nine times over their reps; in view, never. It also hit one tester's chest and fits only one bar size.

media.caption: LevelUp: a compliant PLA clip, and a 1-inch vial press-fit on a 90° arm.
What the lifter sees during a barbell row: the vial between the hands.

blocks.title: My canvas still sold the magnetic version
blocks.text:
I built our business model canvas: beginner lifters buying direct; rec centres, gyms and trainers buying wholesale; a keychain level as a side line (my first brainstorm idea, back again). We priced it at $9.99 retail, $7.99 wholesale. Reading the canvas now, it still pitches a “magnetic clip-on”, and our cost table prices a magnet-and-rubber build at $3.90 a unit. The part we tested was printed plastic and a vial. Next time I'd cost the object on the bench.

Next design round: a clip for 25.5–31.5 mm bars, a shape that clears the chest, rubber for grip, and a thicker fluid for experienced lifters.

media.caption: My business model canvas for LevelUp, June 2025.
